Live an honest and sincere life. Respect your parents, your brothers, and your relatives, and try to live harmoniously with them all. Honor and treat with respect everyone you meet, even those you see only occasionally. Never behave discourteously or selfishly. Never lie. In fact, never say anything that even resembles a lie, even something you heard from someone else.

Until you are forty, avoid every luxury, and never act or think like one above your station in life. In matters of business and moneymaking, however, work harder than anyone else. . . . Always behave as one whose station in life is half that of yours. Although some people may suggest that you [should] be more visible and assertive, ignore all such advice and maintain a low profile. Until you turn fifty, be temperate in all things, and avoid all ostentation and finery, anything, in fact, that might call attention to yourself. Do not cultivate expensive tastes, for you should ignore such things as the tea ceremony, swords, daggers, and fine clothes.

13.
Those with even a small fortune must remember that their duty in life is to devote themselves to their house and its business. They must not become careless, for if they buy what they want, do as they please, and, in general, live sumptuously, they will soon spend that fortune. . . . Although a samurai can draw on the produce of his tenured lands to earn his livelihood, a merchant must rely on the profit from his business, for without that profit, the money in his bags would soon disappear. No matter how much profit he makes and packs into his bags, however, if he continually wastes that money, he may as well pack it into bags full of holes. Remember this.

—from “The Testament of Shimai So–shitsu,” written ca. 1610 in Hakata, Japan, by the head of a prosperous merchant house to his adopted son and heir

explanation: Although all four of these belief systems had a substantial impact on religious and cultural life in seventeenth-century Japan, Confucianism’s emphasis on filial piety and knowing one’s proper place in society is expressed very clearly in the first paragraph of this passage.

stem: Which of the following best describes the social position of Japanese merchants at the time this document was written?
options: (A) They occupied a surprisingly low spot in Japan’s caste system, although their informal influence was rapidly growing.
(B) They suffered from a severe decline in social status after Japan’s unification.
(C) They officially ranked just below the samurai nobility in Japan’s social hierarchy.
(D) They were frequently categorized with artisans and craftsmen despite their growing wealth.
explanation: In contrast to places like Europe, where wealth afforded the merchant classes a large measure of social prestige and even political influence, those social systems in Asia most affected by Confucian ideology assigned a low status to merchants, placing them not just below artisans, but below even peasants. This fact renders (C) and (D) false. On the other hand, this philosophical outlook did not prevent Japan’s merchant class from converting its growing wealth into growing social and political clout. Far from the decline described in (B), Japanese merchants became increasingly rich and more important after the Tokugawa unification of the country.

stem: According to the author, the principal aim of the merchant should be to
options: (A) stand out from one’s competitors through aggressive self-promotion.
(B) accumulate wealth carefully by behaving thriftily and modestly.
(C) seek profit by any means necessary.
(D) serve the public good with acts of philanthropy.

stem: What key development did the battle depicted in the above illustration lead to?
options: (A) The importation of Islam to India
(B) The Mughal conquest of India
(C) The restoration of Hindu rule in India
(D) The rise of the Maratha Confederacy in India
explanation: The question requires understanding of wider context. Even if the battle of Panipat is itself unfamiliar, you should be familiar with Babur as the founder of India’s Mughal dynasty or at least with the fact that the Delhi Sultanate gave way to Mughal rule in the early 1500s. Islam had been present in India for many years before the arrival of the Mughals, so (A) is false, and because the Mughals were themselves Muslim, (C) is also incorrect. The Maratha Confederacy arose years later in resistance to Mughal rule, so (D) is likewise wrong.

stem: For which of the following reasons does gunpowder weaponry—famously used to good effect by the victors of this battle—most likely not appear in this illustration?
options: (A) Presenting the battle as a grand duel highlights Babur’s warrior prowess.
(B) Indian artists of the time tended to idealize the past over the present.
(C) The use of gunpowder weapons was regarded as cowardly in most of India.
(D) Religious strictures forbade the depiction of new technology in the visual arts.
explanation:
While Islam (like Judaism and Christianity) can be interpreted as forbidding the artistic depiction of human beings and other living creatures, there is no such prohibition against picturing technology, making (D) incorrect. While any given artist might or might not share the sentiment described in (B), there is no evidence to suggest that this is the case with the 
Baburnama
, and the same is true about the attitude expressed in (C). Personal combat makes for a more stirring image than an impersonal, macroscopic battle scene, a calculation that would have occurred to the creators of an artistic work whose purpose was to praise a particular political leader, making (A) the best choice.

Baburnama

(B) Indo-Arabic

Although cultural interaction took place between India and all the areas listed in these four answers, the most sustained connection during these years, and the one that gave birth to the most distinctive style, was with Persia. In particular, the genre of miniature painting exemplified by the

stimulus:
Huddling in their small colonial enclaves, the English and Dutch [in the 1600s] were insular and powerless in comparison, managing little more than glimpses of the Indigenous politics that determined events and outcomes. The English thought they could regulate matters of war and peace in the New World, but more often than not, Indians steered them into fighting and financing Indian wars and facilitating truces and treaties with goods and gifts when the fighting stopped. The colonists—whether Spanish, French, English, or Dutch—could be arrogant and

—from Pekka Hämäläinen,

stem: Which of the following best embodies the dynamic described in the above passage?
options: (A) King Philip’s (Metacom’s) War against New England colonists
(B) The Pueblo revolt in present-day New Mexico
(C) Iroquois-Dutch alliance against Hurons and Algonquins in the Beaver Wars
(D) The Powhatan raids against the Jamestown colony
explanation: All four of these events indeed took place. The passage, however, emphasizes a new way of understanding the relationship between European colonizers and Native Americans as more complex than one of straightforward conflict, victimization, and eventual conquest of the latter by the former. Answers (A), (B), and (D) all refer to moments when European and Native Americans clashed in that more straightforward fashion. The Iroquois strategy of forging ties with the Dutch (and later the English) and using them as pieces in their own game against native foes—as in (C)—is a prime example of what the passage has in mind.

stem: Which of the commonly held assumptions about colonial North America does this author’s interpretation of events most directly contradict?
options: (A) Lack of metal tools and gunpowder weaponry handicapped Native Americans in their efforts to resist European colonization.
(B) Diseases brought to North America by European settlers killed well over half of the continent’s indigenous population.
(C) European colonies often survived only because of hospitality and shared knowledge from Native American neighbors.
(D) Native Americans, despite moments of resistance, were largely victims without agency in their interactions with European colonizers.
explanation:
Answers (A), (B), and (C) all touch on important aspects of the interactions between Native Americans and the Europeans who invaded and colonized their lands. The author would not dispute any of these points, and (C), to a degree, supports his argument in that it highlights an active role, not a passive one, played by Native Americans in this relationship. Answer (D), on the other hand, represents a common oversimplification of how Native Americans dealt with European incursions. No one would reasonably argue that Native Americans were 
not
 victimized by colonization, but recent scholarship has emphasized the point that they were not 
only
 victims. Instead, they pursued their own agendas and, in ways not fully appreciated before, used the colonizers for their own purposes, just as they themselves were used by the colonists. The long-term outcome still disadvantaged Native Americans, but they were neither helpless nor passive as the process played out, a point made in answer (D).

stem: This author’s historical approach is best described as
options: (A) Marxist.
(B) Revisionist.
(C) Postmodern.
(D) Traditional.
explanation:
The author is seeking to overturn a long-standing conventional wisdom in his field, which is the opposite of (D) and the exact meaning of (B), the correct answer. (The term 
revisionist
 can be applied to any historical field, and it is a legitimate scholarly approach, except in the area of Holocaust studies, where it is generally taken to mean denying the Holocaust or minimizing the importance of the atrocities associated with it.) Postmodern approaches to history, as in (C), also often seek to undermine traditional understandings of a subject but tend to do so in a more methodologically radical way. Nothing in the passage indicates anything specifically Marxist enough to warrant choosing (A).

stimulus:
The royal court is magnificent and very well organized. When the king goes from one city to another with the people of his court, he rides a camel and the horses are led by hand by servants. When someone wishes to speak to the king, he must kneel before him and bow down; but this is only required of those who have never before spoken to the king, or of ambassadors. This king makes war only upon neighboring enemies and upon those who do not want to pay him tribute. When he has gained a victory, he has all of them—even the children—sold in the market at Timbuktu.

The king is a declared enemy of the Jews. He will not allow any to live in the city. If he hears it said that a Berber merchant does business with them, he confiscates his goods. There are in Timbuktu numerous judges, teachers and priests, all properly appointed by the king. He greatly honors learning.

—Leo Africanus, Christianized Berber diplomat, on the city of Timbuktu, from 
The Description of Africa
, 1526

On the Sultan’s arrival, we were admitted to an audience; but the manner and spirit in which he listened to our message was by no means favorable. He was seated on a low ottoman, covered with costly rugs and cushions of exquisite workmanship; near him lay his bow and arrows. On entering we were conducted into the royal presence by the chamberlains, who grasped our arms. . . . After kissing his hand, we were conducted backwards to the wall opposite his seat, care being taken that we should never turn our backs on him. The Sultan then listened to what I had to say; but the language I used was not at all to his taste, for the demands of our [Habsburg] Majesty breathed a spirit of independence and dignity, which was by no means acceptable to one who deemed that his wish was law. . . .

No distinction is attached to birth among the Turks. It is by merit that men rise in the service, a system which ensures that posts should only be assigned to the competent. Among the Turks, therefore, honours, high posts, and judgeships are the rewards of great ability and good service. If a man be dishonest, or lazy, or careless, he remains an object of contempt. This is the reason they are successful in their undertakings and are daily extending the bounds of their empire. These are not our ideas, with us there is no opening left for merit, but the prestige of birth is the sole key to advancement.

—Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, Flemish diplomat for the Habsburg Empire, excerpt from 
The Turkish Letters
, 1555–1562
stem: What technique of rulership do the monarchs described in these passages both make use of?
options: (A) Rituals of obedience and submission to emphasize the monarch’s personal authority
(B) Lavish gifts to the general population as a means of boosting monarchical popularity
(C) Leadership of armies into battle to display the monarch’s personal bravery
(D) Religious legitimation of the monarch’s divine right to rule
explanation: All four answers describe rulership techniques employed by monarchs at various times and places. There is, however, no mention of war or interaction with commoners, making (B) and (C) poor choices. As Muslim rulers, both the king of Timbuktu and especially the Ottoman sultan (who claimed the status of caliph) would certainly have made political use of Islam, but neither passage discusses this issue directly, so (D) is likewise not suitable. Both authors note that being in the presence of the monarch required them to go through elaborate rituals—kneeling, kissing hands, never turning one’s back—that were deliberately designed to create an impression of the monarch as inherently superior to ordinary subjects and visitors. This is precisely the technique described in (A).

stem: Which of the following best describes first author’s attitude toward the king of Timbuktu?
options: (A) The author admires the king of Timbuktu for his mercy and sense of justice.
(B) The author, a Christian, disapproves of the king of Timbuktu’s practice of Islam.
(C) The author deplores the king of Timbuktu for his antisemitism and his mistreatment of civilians.
(D) The author takes an essentially neutral stance toward the king of Timbuktu and his actions.
explanation: Although the author himself converted from Islam to Christianity, religious persuasion does not seem to be a factor in his assessment of the king of Timbuktu, so (B) is false. The author describes the policies and practices referred to in answers (A) and (C), but seems only mildly positive about the king’s “proper” judges and respect for learning, and is not at all disturbed by the king’s enslavement of civilians or his discrimination against Jews. This matter-of-fact tone makes (D) the best answer.

stem: What internal inconsistency is contained in the second author’s account of the Ottoman sultan’s court?
options: (A) The author criticizes the Ottoman administrative structure but is fond of the sultan himself.
(B) The author’s dislike of Islam contrasts with the religious toleration shown by the sultan.
(C) The author has a somewhat negative view of the sultan but approves of what he sees as meritocracy in the Ottoman system.
(D) The author’s preference for his own nation’s ways clashes with a grudging personal admiration for the Ottoman sultan.
explanation: Whatever his own religious views, the author seems unconcerned in this text about religious differences between the Habsburg Empire he represents and the Ottoman court he is visiting, so (B) is false. His perception of the sultan is not overwhelmingly negative, but he seems put off by the sultan’s haughtiness, making (A) and (D), which describe a personal regard for the sultan, incorrect. Rightly or wrongly, the author sees the Turkish system as rewarding merit and emphasizes this heavily (most likely to encourage this sort of practice back home), making (C) the best choice.
